METADATA.title: Vintage Fender Jazzmaster Value Guide: Prices By Year
METADATA.description: Jazzmaster values from $4,200 to $20,000 across vintage sunburst eras. Compare gold guards, slab boards, CBS changes, custom colors and condition.

OUTLINE: ## Gold Guards And Slab Rosewood Boards
## Original Pickups, Routing And Refinished Bodies
BODY: Vintage Fender Jazzmaster reference values run from $4,200 to $6,000 for typical 1970s sunburst guitars to $12,000 to $20,000 across the early sunburst sales, as of October 2026. Gold guards, slab rosewood boards and original custom colors attract additional collector interest, which a year alone won't capture. For the year and original specification, use my [Fender Jazzmaster dating and identification guide](/fender-jazzmaster-dating-guide/). This guide covers market value and the features that move it. For comparisons with other Fender models, my [vintage Fender value guide](/vintage-fender-value-guide/) brings the guitar and bass price guides together. ## Fender Jazzmaster Values By Year **Reviewed October 2026. US dollars.** Repeated numbers are shared era references, not separate measurements for each year. Read the condition notes with the table. | Year | Value Range | Configuration And Year Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | 1958 | $12,000 to $20,000 | Gold anodized guard and slab rosewood board. | | 1959, Gold Guard | $12,000 to $20,000 | Gold-guard premium exists; shared early-era envelope. | | 1959 Tortoise Guard | $12,000 to $20,000 | Gold to tortoise guard transition; gold-guard premium. | | 1960 | $12,000 to $20,000 | Slab board and tortoise guard on sunburst. | | 1961 | $12,000 to $20,000 | Slab board; original finish and pickups drive placement. | | 1962, Early Slab Board | $12,000 to $20,000 | Shared slab-era reference; slab premium over veneer. | | 1962 Veneer Board | $8,500 to $11,000 | Slab to veneer transition during spring. | | 1963 | $8,500 to $11,000 | Veneer board and unbound neck. | | 1964 | $8,500 to $11,000 | Logo and dot-material transitions; still pre-CBS. | | 1965 | $6,000 to $7,000 | CBS purchase in January; binding arrives late in year. | | 1966 | $5,500 to $9,500 | Bound dots give way to blocks around midyear. | | 1967 | $5,500 to $9,500 | Bound blocks; later logo and headstock changes. | | 1968 | $5,500 to $9,500 | CBS bound-block version; original sunburst. | | 1969 | $5,500 to $9,500 | Late 1960s bound-block configuration. | | 1970 | $4,200 to $6,000 | 1970s sunburst reference; custom colors excluded. | | 1971 | $4,200 to $6,000 | Original pickups and dual circuit retained. | | 1972 | $4,200 to $6,000 | Sunburst and rosewood-board reference. | | 1973 | $4,200 to $6,000 | Weight, wear and original parts affect placement. | | 1974 | $4,200 to $6,000 | Working electronics and original finish assumed. | | 1975 | $4,200 to $6,000 | Unmodified body and original pickups assumed. | | 1976 | $4,200 to $6,000 | Case and refret quality affect the individual guitar. | | 1977 | $4,200 to $6,000 | Later vintage production; reissues excluded. | | 1978 | $4,200 to $6,000 | Sunburst reference; unusual options need individual evidence. | | 1979 | $4,200 to $6,000 | Final year covered here, not the end of all Jazzmaster production. | Gold-guard and slab-board guitars carry collector premiums, but the present sale sample does not isolate either premium as a percentage. The two 1959 rows and the two 1962 rows identify the transitions without inventing a separate price. The 1965 range is a played-sunburst sample, not a ceiling for every early-specification or bound-dot guitar. Its smaller upper figure than the 1966 to 1969 group reflects different condition and configuration samples. A clean transitional 1965 needs a closer match before either range is used. ### Condition Behind The Ranges **1958 To 1961 Sunburst Jazzmaster:** Original sunburst finish and pickups, no disclosed structural repair. Played to very clean; minor knob or switch changes accepted. Gold or tortoise guard as appropriate. Original or period case, with some worn or stiff controls at the lower end. **1962 To 1964 Sunburst Jazzmaster:** Original sunburst finish and pickups, no disclosed structural repairs. Played to clean; refret, one replaced tuner, saddle screws or old owner markings accepted. Original case. **1965 Jazzmaster, Sunburst, Played Originals:** Original finish, pickups, electronics and principal hardware, with original case and ordinary playing wear. Quality refret accepted; removable strap locks with original buttons retained included. Not a museum-quality band. **1966 To 1969 Sunburst Jazzmaster:** Original sunburst finish and pickups, no disclosed structural repair, original case. Played to very clean, with a quality refret allowed. Finish wear and case completeness vary. **1970 To 1979 Sunburst Jazzmaster:** Original sunburst finish and pickups, no disclosed structural repair. Played to very clean; refret, replacement nut or strap buttons and additional shielding accepted. Case originality varies. ### How These Ranges Were Built I checked Reverb Price Guide final prices against the linked instrument descriptions and used Heritage realized results where available. The records span 2023 to 2026, with at least three records per researched era group. Shipping and tax are excluded; auction totals include the buyer's premium. These are sale references, not dealer buying offers. ## Gold Guards And Slab Rosewood Boards The Jazzmaster arrived in 1958 with a gold anodized aluminum guard and a slab rosewood fingerboard. Slab describes the thick, flat-bottomed piece of rosewood on the maple neck. The gold guard gives way to tortoiseshell during 1959, so that year's guitars need more than a serial number beside the price. The gold-guard version carries collector appeal beyond an ordinary later sunburst. The early research envelope includes gold and tortoise guards, and therefore cannot isolate the gold-guard premium numerically. I identify the two 1959 versions in the table rather than suggesting their individual values are identical. Slab boards also carry a premium over later veneer boards in the site's existing model guidance. Veneer is the thinner curved-bottom rosewood board that follows during spring 1962. The two 1962 rows separate those configurations, with the early row using the shared slab-era reference and the later row the veneer-era evidence. An original finish with honest playing wear is a different purchase from a freshly refinished guitar. The 1962 photo shows a worn sunburst instrument, and that wear belongs in its condition assessment. The slab board doesn't cancel the effect of repairs, changed pickups or a replaced neck. ## Pre-CBS And The 1965 Transition Pre-CBS refers to manufacture before CBS bought Fender in January 1965. The ownership date doesn't create a single overnight specification change. Jazzmasters built during 1965 move through changes to knobs, plates and tuners, with fingerboard binding appearing late in the year. Bound dot-marker necks precede the block-inlay version that arrives around mid-1966. A clean bound-dot guitar can therefore interest a different buyer from a worn earlier-style 1965. The table's $6,000 to $7,000 row is a played-sunburst sample, not an upper limit for every transitional example. The later 1960s envelope reaches $9,500 because it includes cleaner guitars and different configurations. That overlap isn't evidence that every 1967 is worth more than every 1965. A price sequence drawn from unlike conditions should never be mistaken for a measured year-by-year decline. The bound neck, block inlays and later fittings define much of the CBS-era appearance. Original pickups and the complete lead and rhythm circuits remain part of the guitar's identity. The Jazzmaster never had the Jaguar's string mute, so a missing mute isn't a value deduction on this model. ## Custom Colors And Matching Headstocks Lake Placid Blue, Charcoal Frost and other factory colors need their own market evidence. A matching headstock can add collector interest when it is original to the instrument. The sunburst price table doesn't establish a universal custom-color multiplier. After the gold-guard period, factory custom colors use white guards, with Olympic White the exception that can be paired with tortoiseshell. Tortoise on Fiesta Red or Lake Placid Blue isn't an ordinary factory pairing under the site's house ruling. That finish-and-guard question belongs in an originality assessment before a color premium is considered. The white guards are nitrate through mid-1965, then non-nitrate white vinyl. Their material belongs with the guitar's production period. The [Fender custom-color authentication guide](/post/fender-custom-color-authentication-guide/) explains the finish evidence behind a factory-color appraisal. The Charcoal Frost photograph shows visible wear on a custom-color guitar. Original wear doesn't establish a single discount, just as a desirable color doesn't guarantee the top price. Finish, originality and the guitar's condition need to describe the same instrument. ## Original Pickups, Routing And Refinished Bodies The broad Jazzmaster pickups are part of the model's appeal. A guitar cut for other pickups has changed wood as well as changed electronics. Restoring the appearance with original-style covers doesn't restore the removed material. For context, the site's [Stratocaster condition benchmarks](/vintage-fender-stratocaster-value-guide/) put a professional refinish at about 45 to 60% of an equivalent excellent-original value, and a very good largely original guitar at about 75 to 90%. These are published Stratocaster benchmarks, not measured Jazzmaster discounts. I use Jazzmaster sale evidence to determine the actual deduction. | Published Stratocaster Benchmark | Share Of An Excellent Original's Value | | --- | --- | | Very Good, Largely Original | About 75 To 90% | | Professional Refinish | About 45 To 60% | A quality refret preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise original guitar while taking it out of the museum-quality category. It differs from a replacement neck, enlarged pickup routes or a full refinish. The price-table conditions already allow some maintenance, so another automatic deduction would count it twice. ## Cases And The 1970s Market The original case and accessories can complete an unusually intact guitar. Early tweed, later brown and black cases belong to different periods, so the case should match the instrument's actual era. The [Jazzmaster evolution guide](/post/fender-jazzmaster-evolution-guide-1958-1971/) covers that wider history. The $4,200 to $6,000 1970s range uses sunburst guitars with original pickups and finish. Quality refrets, a replacement nut or strap buttons and added shielding occur in the evidence. Factory custom colors and unusual options aren't separately priced in that band. These later guitars can provide the familiar Jazzmaster layout without the early gold-guard or slab-board collector price. A working vibrato, intact controls and a comfortable neck affect their usefulness as instruments. Original parts and a clear repair history help explain a particular asking or selling figure. For an individual appraisal, send front and back photographs, the headstock, bridge, case and any known changes through the [free guitar appraisal](/free-appraisal/) page. Keep removed original parts with it. A dealer offer includes preparation, selling costs and margin, so it won't simply repeat the top retail reference.

mainEntity.name: How Much Is A Vintage Fender Jazzmaster Worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vintage Fender Jazzmaster reference values run from $4,200 to $6,000 for typical 1970s sunburst guitars to $12,000 to $20,000 across the early sunburst sales, as of October 2026. Gold guards, slab rosewood boards and original custom colors attract additional collector interest, which a year alone won't capture.

mainEntity.name: Does A Slab Board Increase Jazzmaster Value?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The site's model guidance identifies a collector premium for slab-board Jazzmasters. The 1962 table separates slab and veneer versions, but the evidence does not establish a universal percentage premium.

No. CBS bought Fender in January 1965, while specification changes continued through the year. Binding arrives late in 1965 and block inlays follow around mid-1966. The actual configuration is more useful than a blanket pre-CBS label.

mainEntity.name: Does A Refinish Change Fender Jazzmaster Value?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A full refinish removes the original finish that collectors pay for. The sunburst ranges assume original finish; a refinished Jazzmaster needs matching altered-guitar evidence rather than an automatic deduction borrowed from another model.

mainEntity.name: How Can I Get My Fender Jazzmaster Appraised?

acceptedAnswer.text: Send clear front and back photographs, both sides of the headstock, the pickups, bridge, case and any known repairs. Keep removed original parts with the instrument and include the history you know. Those details support an individual appraisal.
